questions.q: Match each firm to its main job.
pairs: Current accounts, savings and mortgages for the public
Advising companies on deals and raising money
Investing other people's money for a fee
Buying and selling on behalf of clients
questions.why: Each type of firm handles one part of moving and managing money.

questions.q: Match each body to its role.
pairs: Makes sure firms treat customers fairly and markets are honest
Makes sure banks and insurers are strong enough to survive shocks
Pays compensation if an authorised firm fails
questions.why: Conduct (FCA), safety (PRA, part of the Bank of England), complaints (Ombudsman), compensation (FSCS).

questions.q: Why are asset managers called the 'buy side'?
options: They buy investments with the money they manage
They only ever buy and never sell
They buy companies outright
They buy services from shops
questions.why: Asset managers buy investments; investment banks sell them services and products, so they're the sell side.

questions.q: Which is a core job of the financial system?
options: Moving money from savers to people and firms who can use it
Setting the prices of food in shops
Collecting income tax
Running the NHS
questions.why: Finance moves money from savers to users, handles payments, manages risk and prices assets.

questions.q: Building societies are owned by their members rather than by outside shareholders.
questions.why: They're mutuals: owned by their savers and borrowers.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a usual job of an investment bank?
options: Running your personal current account
Advising on mergers and acquisitions
Helping companies issue shares and bonds
Trading for big clients
questions.why: Current accounts are retail banking. Investment banks advise, raise money and trade for institutions.

questions.q: Put the journey of a pension contribution in order.
items: Employer deducts it from your pay
Asset manager invests it in the fund
The fund buys company shares on a stock exchange
questions.why: Payroll, provider, fund manager, market. Each step adds a small cost.

questions.q: Before handing money to a financial firm, what's the best quick check?
options: Look it up on the FCA register
Check it has a nice website
Ask how high its returns are
See if it advertises on social media
questions.why: The FCA register shows whether a firm is authorised and what it may do. Watch for clones using real names.

questions.q: Roughly how big are UK financial services, on government figures?
options: About 9% of economic output and 1.2 million jobs
About 50% of output
Under 1% of output
Exactly half of all UK jobs
questions.why: About 9% of output and 1.2 million jobs (2025), more if related professional services are included.

questions.q: Explain how your savings in a bank or fund end up helping the wider economy.

ideas.label: Banks and funds pass savers' money to borrowers or companies
Those firms or people use it productively: build, hire, buy homes, grow

questions.model: Banks lend savers' deposits on as mortgages and business loans, and funds buy shares and bonds in companies and governments. Those borrowers use the money productively: buying homes, building factories, hiring staff and growing, and they pay savers back with interest, dividends and growth.
questions.why: Finance links people with money now to people who can put it to work.

tests.answer: The bank lends it to businesses and home buyers, who use it to build, hire and grow.

questions.q: Explain why the long chain of firms between you and your investments makes fees important.

ideas.label: Each firm in the chain takes a fee or spread
Small charges add up and reduce your return over time

questions.model: Every firm in the chain (provider, fund manager, broker, custodian) takes a fee or a spread. Each looks small, but together they add up and, compounded over years, can take a big slice of your return.
questions.why: A long chain means many small charges.

tests.answer: Each firm takes a fee, and together they add up and reduce your return over time.
